body.text: Singapore rolls out new dating app FirstDate, as marriage and fertility rates fall
Government-funded "date quests", a pioneering matching algorithm and a platform only available for public servants.
Singapore's FirstDate dating app aims to boost connection as fertility rates hit a record low and marriage rates continue to decline in the city-state.
It launched this week for civil servants aged 21 to 35 but not everyone is convinced it will be successful.
Here's how FirstDate works, how it might affect marriage and fertility rates, and how the app fits into a broader pattern in Asia.
How does FirstDate work?
Only civil servants who verify their details through Singpass, the national identity system, can use FirstDate.
They fill out questions about their interests, habits and values before the Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage algorithm uses these answers to try and match suitable partners.
The algorithm was designed by American mathematicians David Gale and Lloyd Shapley, who said in 1962 that it was designed to create matches based on people's preferences.
FirstDate offers one match at a time, rather than a feed of profiles and endless scrolling.
Once users match, they have three days to decide whether to connect.
If users choose to go on a date, they can agree to certain activities, or "date quests", which the government will provide vouchers for.
Users can then provide feedback on how their dates went.
A very Singaporean idea?
Tingting Liu studies dating culture at the University of Technology Sydney and saw parallels between FirstDate and other apps in China.
She said it was similar to Chinese platform Qingteng Love, which centres on educational credentials and targets highly educated young people.
Another app, Er'gou, verifies identity using education history and courts tech firm employees and finance sector workers.
She called these apps "credentialised intimacy" platforms.

"Most dating apps already tell you someone's occupation and education, and users inevitably make judgements from these, but FirstDate is quite clever because it simply brings one of those filters to the front: everyone is already a public officer," Ms Liu said.
"What interests me more is the combination of a very pragmatic approach to heterosexual partner selection with a particularly Singaporean faith in systems, verification and efficiency," she added.
She viewed the app as trying to manage uncertainty by limiting choice.
Shared employment signalled similar schedules and expectations about career and stability, which may interest users, Ms Liu said.
Pan Wang, an associate professor of Chinese and Asian Studies at UNSW, said FirstDate showed the government getting "more involved in people's private lives" and "taking the role of big parent".
She said historically parents, relatives or communities would introduce people.
"The underlying social function [of FirstDate] remains quite similar, like pouring old wine in new bottles," she said.
Is FirstDate safer than other apps?
Ms Wang's research on digital parental matchmaking in east Asia revealed that trust was a selling point and FirstDate's verification would likely boost people's trust in it.
She said concepts like FirstDate suited societies where marriage was still institutionalised.

"In Singapore, China and other Asian societies, partner choice is not really shaped only by individual attraction but also by a lot of other things like education, career and family background," she said.
Apps like FirstDate acted as a "mediator", she said, making awkward questions easier to ask.
In the wider market, she said "dating has been highly commercialised and manipulated by technology — what differs with FirstDate is it is driven by the state".
Ms Liu agreed.

"What we are seeing now, unfortunately, is a much less romantic dating environment … I would say that the space for surprise has narrowed: platforms increasingly anticipate preferences, filter possibilities and steer users toward people who already appear compatible," she said.
Will it raise births and marriage rates?
Singapore's fertility rate fell to a record low of 0.87 children per woman in 2025, down from 0.97 in 2024.
The city-state recorded 24,688 marriages in 2025, a 6.2 per cent drop from 2024.
Experts were sceptical that FirstDate would drastically boost fertility or marriage rates.
"The causes such as housing costs, surging living costs and work pressure are still there, so this algorithmic matching alone wouldn't really help to tackle the root problem," Ms Wang said.
"It could help people to partner up, but it may not necessarily help to address the decline in birthrates," she said.
GovTech Singapore, the government agency that designed FirstDate, declined an interview and to answer questions from the ABC about the app's aims.

Earlier this year, Singapore's prime minister, Lawrence Wong, announced financial incentives to help parents start and raise families, including $S70,000 ($78,000) in support for every child from birth to the age of 17.
In Japan, an AI-powered dating app launched by the Tokyo government in 2024 to lift Japan's low birthrate led to 265 marriages.
Seoul's local government relaunched its matchmaking program in August after 126 couples were matched since its inception in 2024.
